Every entry here must be committed BEFORE the run it judges. The git history is the

What a commit buys is that moving a threshold becomes a visible diff instead of a
Each threshold carries a derivation. A threshold without one is an arbitrary constant
wearing a harness, and an examiner's first question is 'who chose this number'.

C-6.name: Held-out probe pool
C-6.question: Are the published pilot metrics training metrics rather than generalization metrics?
background: Every metric in the project is computed on the same 4,096-point pool the chain trains
on. At B = 4096 the students train on all of it, so the tau0.5/1.0/2.0_b4096 rows of
the pilot table are training metrics by construction. Three of those rows are cited
as evidence in the public README.
C-6.metric: abs(agree_gen0 on probe pool - agree_gen0 on training pool) at generation 25
C-6.fails_if: metric exceeds threshold in any condition
derivation: Published generation-25 agreements at B = 4096 are 0.219, 0.164 and 0.132 for
tau = 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0. Adjacent conditions are separated by 0.055 and 0.032.
A probe-versus-training gap of 0.05 is therefore the scale at which the temperature
ordering could reorder - that is, the scale at which a stated conclusion changes.
Anything smaller moves numbers without moving claims.
verdict_if_failed: The published pilot table is a table of training metrics. Relabel it as such, and
rerun on the probe pool before any claim rests on those rows.
sanity_check: At B = 128 the students train on 128 of 4,096 points, so training-pool and probe-pool
metrics should already agree closely. A large gap THERE means the probe pool is built
wrong, not that the finding is real.

C-2.name: No chaining
C-2.question: Does iteration do anything that a single distillation step does not?
background: No control has ever compared a chain generation against a student distilled once
directly from generation 0. If chain-generation 5 looks like a fresh one-step
student, iteration is doing nothing and 'iterated distillation' is the wrong
C-2.reference_distribution: one-step students distilled directly from generation 0 at the same bottleneck

sanity.condition: chain-generation 1 lies inside the one-step reference's central 95%
sanity.meaning_if_failed: the control is misconfigured, not a finding - generation 1 IS a one-step student by construction

A.condition: some generation g <= 25 falls below the one-step reference's 2.5th percentile
A.meaning_if_failed: iteration changes nothing about the learned function

B.condition: some generation g <= 25 falls below the one-step reference's 2.5th percentile
B.meaning_if_failed: alphabet contraction is a one-step effect, not an iterated one

derivation: The 2.5th percentile is the one-sided form of the two-sided 95% intervals already
used in analysis/seed_stability_stats.py. It is the repository's existing statistical
convention rather than a new number introduced for this control.
verdict_if_failed: If gates A and B BOTH fail: hard stop. Iteration is doing nothing measurable, the
iterated framing is unsupported, and the semester's spine needs rethinking before any
If gate B alone fails: the contraction headline has a one-step explanation, and
C-4's minority-collapse concern (Fang et al. 2021, PNAS) arrives early. At B = 128
a one-step student already sees only about 2.6 examples per class.

C-3.name: One-step fidelity baseline
C-3.question: Is the loss from a single distillation step an optimization artifact or an information limit?
background: RESEARCH-PLAN.md section 4.1 specifies C-3 as agreement with generation 0 after a
SINGLE distillation step at B = 4096, and says: 'whatever that number is, it is the
floor against which all downstream decay must be read.'
C-2 already measured the number: 0.230 on held-out inputs at B = 4096, over 50
one-step students at 1500 training steps. So the floor exists. What C-2 did not
test is whether that floor MOVES with the training budget.
This matters because Stanton et al. attribute one-step teacher-student discrepancy
to optimization rather than information loss. If they are right here, the floor is a
property of how long we train, not of what the bottleneck destroys, and every decay
number in this project has been read against a budget-dependent baseline without
C-3.metric: one-step agree_gen0 at B = 4096 on the held-out probe pool, as training steps increase from the standard 1500
C-3.reference_provenance: logs/c2_no_chaining.json, 50 one-step students at 1500 steps, probe pool, 95% CI
C-3.fails_if: one-step agreement at 4x the training budget (6000 steps) exceeds 0.243, the upper bound of the 1500-step reference interval
derivation: The threshold is the upper bound of the measured reference interval, not a chosen
number. Run-to-run spread across 50 one-step students at the standard budget is
0.022 wide. A budget increase that pushes the mean outside that interval has moved
the floor by more than the noise it was measured with; one that does not, has not.
4x is the smallest multiplier that clearly separates a real trend from noise at this
interval width, and 6000 steps is about 11 s per student on this machine, so the
sweep is affordable at n = 20 per budget.
verdict_if_failed: The one-step floor is optimization-dependent, not an information limit. Consequences:
every decay claim must be reported against a budget-matched floor rather than against
generation 0 alone; the 1500-step choice becomes a reported parameter rather than an
implementation detail; and the C-2 escape generations (4, 7, 16) need re-checking,
since they are defined relative to a reference distribution that itself moves.
This does not invalidate C-2 — the chain still leaves the reference — but it changes
verdict_if_passed: The floor is an information limit at this budget. 0.230 stands as the number all
downstream decay is read against, and the 1500-step choice is not load-bearing.
sanity_check: The 1500-step arm of this sweep must reproduce the C-2 reference mean of 0.230 within
its interval. If it does not, the sweep is not measuring the same thing C-2 measured
and nothing else in it can be read.
